scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

Byzantine is a modern label for the Eastern Roman state; 395 is the map’s conventional division date, not a sudden founding of a new people. The capital began as Constantine’s Roman city in 330. Roman self-identity and growing dominance of Greek distinguished. In 1204–1261 the map uses a single continuing label despite Latin rule at Constantinople and rival Byzantine courts elsewhere. The 1400–1492 imported polygon extends beyond the 1453 capital conquest; historical dateBasis preserves the attested cutoff while geometry remains unchanged/unverified.

Met essay says Mistra and Trebizond fell in 1460, but Trebizond is commonly dated 1461; neither later date is included until separately checked. 1453 marks the court/capital end, not extinction of Eastern Christian communities. No Ottoman successor link added without exact event-year target geometry/identity verification.

UNESCO Istanbul property mixes Byzantine and later Ottoman buildings. Card names only the fifth-century walls and 532–537 Hagia Sophia for Byzantine builders; later timber homes, Ottoman complexes, and modern functions are not back-projected. The cistern study gives at least 33 within a later palace enclosure, not a citywide count or proof all operated at once.

Egyptian child tunic and bone figure are province-specific. Bone figure may be toy or amulet; not certain childhood play or a known owner. Met bread stamp served Eucharistic preparation, not all ordinary bread. Barcın and Kadıkalesi isotope analysis samples 38 people across distinct centuries and settings; inferred dietary spread, not individual recipes or empire-wide diet.

Marea sixth-century Egyptian latrines discharged into a lake; card does not call this hygienic, universal, or proof of flush toilets. Hospital mentioned on an ostracon near 600; no medical outcome or admission policy claimed. Cambridge schooling chapter chiefly concerns higher/fee-paying education and not universal literacy. Religious calendar source describes medieval Orthodox laity, not every subject or minority.

Greek writing sample is exactly the legible string ΒΟΗΘΕΙ ΤΩ ΣΩ ΔΟΥΛΩ in the Museum of Byzantine Culture transcription of Eustathius’s tenth-century Thessaloniki seal. The abbreviated first word +Κ(ΥΡΙ)Ε is explained but not silently expanded as carved text. No claim that all residents could read Greek.

All narrative author-checked and awaiting independent review. Map polygons and imported dates are unverified; no border edits. Region crosses Europe and western Asia, but the record was unassigned in the research queue when claimed; QWEN-owned Asia-only entries remain untouched.

proposedOverrides.summary: The people of the eastern Roman Empire called themselves Romans. From Constantinople they governed a changing realm for more than a millennium, building domes and walls, copying books, caring for children and debating faith. The imperial capital fell to the Ottomans in 1453, while its communities and traditions continued.

identityEvidence.assessment: Imported geometry identifies the map label and rounded snapshot period only; territory has not been historically verified. At 1200–1279 it obscures Latin rule of Constantinople in 1204–1261; at 1400–1492 it outlasts the 1453 court.
